categories.label: Insect
facts: An estimated 40% of insect species are in decline globally, with populations dropping by 75% in some regions over the past 30 years.
Insects form the base of most terrestrial food webs. Their disappearance triggers cascading collapse across entire ecosystems.
Flying insect populations have declined by more than 75% in protected natural areas in Germany over 27 years — and the trend is global.
The drivers are well understood: habitat loss, pesticide use, light pollution, invasive species, and climate change.
One in three bites of food humans eat depends on insect pollination. Their decline threatens agriculture directly.

categories.label: Invertebrate
facts: Freshwater molluscs are among the most imperiled groups on Earth — over 40% of species are extinct or critically endangered.
Marine invertebrates face mounting pressure from ocean acidification, which dissolves the calcium carbonate that forms their shells.
Coral reefs — built by tiny invertebrate animals — have declined by 50% globally since 1950 and face near-total collapse by 2100 under current warming trajectories.
Over 600 mollusc species have gone extinct since 1500 CE, more than any other animal group on record.
Many invertebrate extinctions go undocumented — scientists estimate far more species vanish than are ever catalogued.

categories.label: Plant
facts: Two out of every five plant species on Earth are threatened with extinction — a higher proportion than birds, mammals, or reptiles.
Plant extinctions are occurring at 500 times the historical background rate.
Each plant extinction can trigger secondary extinctions of the insects, birds, and animals that depended exclusively on it.
Forests, home to most terrestrial plant diversity, are disappearing at roughly 10 million hectares per year.
Plants produce the oxygen we breathe, regulate climate, and form the base of nearly every food web on Earth.

categories.label: Mammal
facts: 26% of all mammal species are currently threatened with extinction, according to the IUCN Red List.
The total biomass of wild land mammals has declined by over 80% since the rise of human civilization.
Large mammals — 'megafauna' — have been disproportionately impacted. Their loss reshapes entire ecosystems they once maintained.
Since 1500 CE, at least 85 mammal species have gone extinct, including the thylacine, the West African black rhino, and the baiji dolphin.
Habitat destruction and hunting remain the primary drivers, but the illegal wildlife trade now kills more mammals than any other single cause.

categories.label: Bird
facts: Nearly 1 in 8 bird species is threatened with extinction. Since 1970, North America alone has lost 3 billion birds — a 29% decline.
Migratory bird populations have declined by up to 37% globally since the 1970s, disrupting pollination and pest control across two continents.
Window collisions, cats, and vehicle strikes kill between 1.3 and 4 billion birds in the U.S. every year.
At least 160 bird species have gone extinct since 1500 CE — more than any other vertebrate group.
Island bird species have been hardest hit: invasive rats and cats have driven dozens of unique island birds to extinction.

categories.label: Fish
facts: Freshwater fish are among the most endangered vertebrates — over a third of all species are threatened with extinction.
One-third of all shark and ray species are threatened with extinction, primarily due to overfishing and finning.
Ocean dead zones caused by agricultural runoff have quadrupled since 1950, suffocating entire fish communities.
Dams and water diversions have fragmented river ecosystems, pushing migratory fish like salmon and sturgeon toward collapse.
Since 1970, monitored freshwater fish populations have declined by an average of 76%.

categories.label: Amphibian
facts: Amphibians are the most threatened class of vertebrates on Earth — over 40% of known species are in decline.
The chytrid fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) has driven at least 90 amphibian species to extinction since the 1970s, the largest documented disease-driven vertebrate collapse in history.
Frogs, salamanders, and caecilians are sensitive indicators of ecosystem health. Their disappearance often signals broader collapse.
Amphibians have existed for over 350 million years, surviving five mass extinctions — but are now disappearing at 211 times the background rate.
Wetland drainage has destroyed much of their habitat. More than 35% of the world's wetlands have been lost since 1970.

categories.label: Reptile
facts: 21% of all reptile species are currently threatened with extinction.
Sea turtles, which have roamed the oceans for over 100 million years, now face threats from plastic pollution, fishing bycatch, egg collection, and rising sea levels that drown nesting beaches.
The illegal wildlife trade targets reptiles heavily — particularly turtles, geckos, and chameleons prized in the exotic pet trade.
All seven species of sea turtle are classified as vulnerable, endangered, or critically endangered.
Climate change is shifting the sex ratios of reptile populations: warmer sand produces mostly female sea turtles, threatening long-term reproductive viability.
